pathway.title: Programming
pathway.description: Build clear, maintainable software from Python foundations through advanced object models, concurrency, security, packaging, persistence, and architecture.

course.title: Python Programming — Advanced
course.short_description: An advanced Python course focused on the data model, generic contracts, concurrency, resilience, performance, secure boundaries, packaging, persistence, observability, and architecture.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Python Programming — Intermediate or equivalent experience with modules, classes, type hints, files, tests, exceptions, and basic concurrency.
learning_outcomes: Design generic, protocol-oriented Python APIs and controlled object-model extensions.
Coordinate asynchronous and parallel work with explicit lifecycle, cancellation, backpressure, and failure policies.
Measure performance and build secure, reproducible Python packages.
Implement transactional persistence and safe external boundaries.
Architect, observe, test, and review a maintainable advanced Python system.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

topics.title: Use advanced type systems and generic protocols
topics.description: Type annotations can express reusable contracts with TypeVar, Protocol, overloads, and generic containers.

lesson.title: Use advanced type systems and generic protocols
objectives: Explain why a TypeVar preserves the relationship between input and output.
Use a Protocol to describe behavior without requiring inheritance.
Identify what still needs runtime validation.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Type annotations can express reusable contracts with TypeVar, Protocol, overloads, and generic containers. A protocol describes behavior rather than inheritance, allowing structurally compatible implementations. Generic functions should preserve useful relationships between input and output types instead of replacing everything with Any. Static checking is valuable, but annotations remain documentation unless a tool or explicit runtime validation enforces them. Advanced Python work requires more than knowing syntax: it requires choosing a precise contract, understanding runtime behavior, and measuring whether the design is appropriate. Start by stating what the component accepts, what it returns, and which failures are possible. Keep side effects at visible boundaries and make the core behavior deterministic where practical. The standard library is deliberately broad, but using a powerful feature does not automatically make a program better. Prefer the simplest design that meets the requirement, document important trade-offs, and test both ordinary and boundary cases. When concurrency, reflection, persistence, or optimization is involved, reason about resource ownership, ordering, cancellation, and observability. Treat examples as small experiments: predict the result, run them, and then explain why the result follows from Python's data model. A production-quality implementation also considers maintainability, security, portability, and privacy rather than optimizing only for a clever demonstration.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
class SizedSource(Protocol[T]):
    def first(self) -> T: ...

def first_or_none(values: list[T]) -> T | None:
    return values[0] if values else None

print(first_or_none(["typed", "contract"]))
print(first_or_none([]))

topics.title: Coordinate asynchronous work with asyncio
topics.description: Asyncio uses cooperative concurrency: an event loop schedules coroutines, and an await gives other tasks a chance to run while waiting.

lesson.title: Coordinate asynchronous work with asyncio
objectives: Define and run a coroutine safely.
Use gather, timeout, or cancellation with an explicit ownership policy.
Distinguish I/O concurrency from CPU parallelism.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Asyncio uses cooperative concurrency: an event loop schedules coroutines, and an await gives other tasks a chance to run while waiting. Async code is useful for many I/O-bound operations, not for making CPU-bound work automatically faster. Avoid blocking calls inside the event loop; use an async API or move blocking work to an executor. Manage task lifetime, cancellation, timeouts, and exceptions explicitly so work does not continue after its owner has gone away. When concurrency, reflection, persistence, or optimization is involved, reason about resource ownership, ordering, cancellation, and observability. blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch(label, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return label

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("A", 0), fetch("B", 0))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

topics.title: Design cancellation, backpressure, and resilient pipelines
topics.description: A concurrent pipeline needs more than producers and consumers.

lesson.title: Design cancellation, backpressure, and resilient pipelines
objectives: Explain bounded capacity and backpressure.
Use a clear shutdown or cancellation signal.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A concurrent pipeline needs more than producers and consumers. Backpressure prevents fast producers from exhausting memory, cancellation stops work that no longer matters, and retries must distinguish transient failures from permanent invalid input. Bounded queues make capacity visible. Use idempotent operations when retries are possible, record a correlation identifier for observability, and ensure cleanup runs when cancellation occurs. Resilience is a contract about what the system does under pressure, not a blanket retry loop. lesson.title: Build secure parsers and safe subprocess boundaries

blocks.title: Understand the idea

Parse with a strict grammar or a safe standard-library parser, validate size and shape, and reject ambiguous values. subprocess should receive an argument list rather than a shell command string when shell interpretation is unnecessary. from pathlib import PurePosixPath

def safe_name(value):
    path = PurePosixPath(value)
    if path.is_absolute() or ".." in path.parts:
        raise ValueError("unsafe path")
    return path.name

lesson.title: Observe systems with structured logging and tracing
objectives: Choose stable structured event fields.
Propagate correlation context across a boundary.
Test observability without leaking sensitive values.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Advanced software needs evidence when behavior crosses threads, tasks, processes, and persistence boundaries. Structured logs should carry stable event names, severity, correlation identifiers, and safe fields. Metrics answer questions about rates, latency, and resource use; traces connect a request across components. The standard logging module can provide the foundation, but the design of messages matters more than printing more lines. Avoid secrets and high-cardinality uncontrolled values. Make failure paths observable without changing the program's public result, and test that important events are emitted at the correct boundary. Advanced Python work requires more than knowing syntax: it requires choosing a precise contract, understanding runtime behavior, and measuring whether the design is appropriate. Start by stating what the component accepts, what it returns, and which failures are possible. Keep side effects at visible boundaries and make the core behavior deterministic where practical. The standard library is deliberately broad, but using a powerful feature does not automatically make a program better. Prefer the simplest design that meets the requirement, document important trade-offs, and test both ordinary and boundary cases. When concurrency, reflection, persistence, or optimization is involved, reason about resource ownership, ordering, cancellation, and observability. Treat examples as small experiments: predict the result, run them, and then explain why the result follows from Python's data model. A production-quality implementation also considers maintainability, security, portability, and privacy rather than optimizing only for a clever demonstration.

logger.info("%s %s", record["event"], record["task_id"])
print(record["ok"])

blocks.body: An advanced system combines contracts, concurrency or persistence, packaging, tests, security, and observability without losing a clear architecture. Begin with the domain and boundaries, then choose technology that serves the requirements. Make ownership explicit: who creates tasks, who closes resources, who commits data, and who handles cancellation. Use architecture tests or focused integration tests to protect important boundaries. blocks.title: Operable Async Task Service Core
blocks.purpose: Design and implement a small offline task-service core that demonstrates advanced Python architecture, asynchronous coordination, safe persistence, packaging, tests, and observability without exposing a network endpoint.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional task data only; do not collect names, contact details, credentials, or learner identifiers.
Keep the project offline and local. Use SQLite or in-memory state for demonstrations and never invoke shell commands from untrusted input.
Do not log secrets or unnecessary sensitive values; document resource, cancellation, and data-retention limits.
requirements: Define a typed domain model and clear public interfaces for task operations.
Provide a SQLite repository using parameterized SQL, constraints, and explicit transactions.
Provide an async coordinator with timeout and cancellation behavior, without blocking the event loop.
Separate domain, persistence, orchestration, and entry-point responsibilities.
Add structured safe logging with a correlation identifier at a meaningful boundary.
Create deterministic unit and integration tests for success, failure, cancellation, duplicate, rollback, and empty cases.
Add package metadata, setup instructions, compatibility notes, and an architecture decision record.
suggested_steps: Write domain contracts and pure validation tests first.
Implement the repository with schema constraints and transaction tests.
Add async orchestration with bounded work, timeout, cancellation, and cleanup.
Add safe observability and package the project in a clean environment.
Run the full test suite and complete a security, privacy, and operability review.
success_checks: The domain remains testable without a live service or external account.
Duplicate and invalid data fail safely without partial committed state.
Async work has explicit timeout, cancellation, and resource ownership behavior.
Logs are useful and contain no secrets or unnecessary personal data.
The package can be installed and tested from documented clean-environment steps.

Reproducible setup, compatibility notes, architecture decisions, limitations, and privacy review.
